results.title: South Korea-Based Seoyon E-HWA Plans Chatham County, Georgia, Manufacturing Plant - Area Development
results.content:
Seoyon E-HWA, a South Korea-based global auto parts supplier that manufactures both interior and exterior components, will establish a new manufacturing facility in Chatham County, Georgia. The $76 million project is expected to create roughly 500 jobs.  
  
 The new facility will be located at the Savannah Chatham Manufacturing Center and will produce automotive interior parts such as door trims, headlining, and tailgate trims. Production is scheduled to begin in October 2024. [...] Established in 1972, Seoyon E-Hwa operates 32 corporations in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. The company supplies door trim, headlining, seats, C/PAD, bumpers, and other parts to Hyundai Motor Group, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Ford, Volkswagen, and more. results.title: Tariffs send shockwaves through Georgia's industries
results.content:
Remaining in effect, thus far, are a 25% tariff on imported cars and car parts and a 125% tariff on all Chinese goods — both of which, observers say, could deal an immediate blow to Georgia industries.

image description

### Car parts chaos

Not all industries are feeling as optimistic as the chamber about the sudden tariff change. [...] The White House initially established 10% tariffs on imports from all countries, along with higher “reciprocal” tariffs targeting nations such as China, Vietnam and members of the European Union that levy tariffs on U.S. goods. Mexico and Canada — Georgia’s top export destinations — were spared from the new tariffs. [...] Chinese tariffs could especially affect local businesses, the Georgia chamber noted. China was the third largest buyer of local goods last year at $3 billion, behind Canada and Mexico, and the second highest importer to Georgia at $17.2 billion.

On April 3, the chamber published a report outlining the impacts local industries may experience from the tariffs, including higher prices for car parts and steel, a squeeze on crop imports and possible slowdowns at the state’s bustling ports.
